coverage_gaps: No live market-pricing check was performed in this Layer 1A pass; valuation, consensus expectations, short interest, and recent price moves require separate market-data validation.
Geographic coverage is still US-heavy because the pilot universe centers on US-listed and global mega-cap companies; Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Europe, and A-share suppliers should be added in Layer 1B.

Private-company exposure is important in AI infrastructure, especially model labs, data-center developers, optical component suppliers, and server ODM relationships; public-market mapping may miss private chokepoints.

The nuclear and power theme needs stricter timeline separation: near-term AI power demand can benefit grid equipment and firm-power contracts, while new nuclear/SMR deployment may have much longer permitting, financing, and fuel-cycle lead times.
Software monetization evidence is weaker and more company-specific than semiconductor infrastructure evidence; Layer 1B should distinguish proven consumption revenue from AI narrative.

evidence.claim: The International Energy Agency stated that electricity consumption from data centres, artificial intelligence, and the cryptocurrency sector could double by 2026, with data centres and data transmission networks each accounting for about 1% to 1.3% of global electricity use in 2022.
evidence.source_title: IEA Electricity 2024: Analysis and forecast to 2026

evidence.claim: NVIDIA reports a Data Center business segment and described data-center demand as a major driver of fiscal 2024 revenue growth, including demand for accelerated computing and generative AI.
Microsoft's FY2024 Annual Report discusses continued investment in cloud and AI infrastructure and identifies data centers and other infrastructure as major capital expenditure requirements.
TSMC provides annual-report disclosure for its foundry business and advanced packaging capabilities, making it a core source for checking leading-edge manufacturing and packaging capacity claims.
ASML identifies lithography systems, including EUV systems, as critical semiconductor manufacturing equipment and reports order, backlog, and geographic risk information in its annual reports.
Arista Networks reports that its cloud networking products serve large-scale cloud and data-center customers, making it a relevant public-market source for AI networking exposure checks.
Vertiv describes its business as critical digital infrastructure technologies and services, including power management and thermal management for data centers and other critical environments.
Amazon reports AWS as a major cloud segment and discusses capital expenditures for infrastructure supporting technology and content, fulfillment, and AWS capacity.
evidence.source_title: Amazon Annual Reports, Proxies and Shareholder Letters

evidence.claim: Alphabet reports Google Cloud as a segment and discloses technical infrastructure investment, including servers and data centers, in its annual filings.
Meta reports significant capital expenditures for data centers, servers, network infrastructure, and AI-related infrastructure in its annual filings and investor disclosures.

memory_update.text: AI theme should be tracked as a system expansion from model demand to cloud deployment, accelerator silicon, HBM/advanced packaging, networking, power/cooling/grid, and software monetization.

HBM plus advanced packaging is a high-priority AI chokepoint candidate because it combines high technical difficulty, supplier concentration, qualification requirements, and capacity expansion lead times.
Data-center power and cooling should be treated as an AI infrastructure node, not merely a utility subtheme, because rack density and total site power can constrain deployment.
AI networking and optical interconnect deserve separate coverage from accelerators because cluster scaling can shift bottlenecks into switch silicon, NICs, optics, DSPs, lasers, and cabling.
Layer 1B should expand beyond the pilot universe into Asian memory, substrate, OSAT, server ODM, optics, and semiconductor equipment suppliers.
Layer 1B should add a market-pricing check to distinguish under-researched bottlenecks from already-consensus AI beneficiaries.

summary: AI is best decomposed as a multi-layer infrastructure buildout rather than a single software or chip theme. The strongest first-pass chokepoint map runs from model demand and cloud deployment into accelerator silicon, HBM/advanced packaging, high-speed networking, data-center power/cooling/grid interconnection, and enterprise/industrial AI software adoption. At Layer 1A, the goal is not to select securities but to identify where incremental AI demand meets scarce capacity, long qualification cycles, high capital intensity, or regulatory constraints.

demand_drivers: Hyperscaler training and inference demand for large language models, recommendation systems, search, coding assistants, advertising optimization, and AI agents.
Enterprise adoption of generative AI through cloud platforms, copilots, data platforms, workflow automation, cybersecurity, customer support, and industrial analytics.
Sovereign and regulated-sector AI demand from governments, defense, healthcare, financial services, and national compute infrastructure programs.
Edge and on-device AI demand in PCs, smartphones, vehicles, robotics, factory automation, and embedded systems.
Second-order infrastructure demand from AI data-center density: power distribution, backup power, cooling, grid connections, substations, transmission, land, water, and permitting.
theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Start with the system bottlenecks, not the most visible AI tickers. Build parallel public-market baskets for: 1) AI accelerator and custom silicon exposure; 2) HBM, advanced packaging, substrates, EDA, test, and semiconductor equipment; 3) AI networking and optical interconnect; 4) data-center power, cooling, grid construction, and energy supply; 5) cloud hyperscalers and colocation operators as demand aggregators; 6) AI software and automation platforms where revenue evidence can be separated from narrative. For each basket, prioritize companies with verifiable revenue exposure, customer qualification evidence, capacity expansion evidence, backlog/order evidence, pricing power or margin evidence, and falsifiable leading indicators.
supply_side_constraints: Advanced-node foundry capacity and wafer starts for leading-edge AI accelerators and custom ASICs.
HBM supply, CoWoS/advanced packaging capacity, interposers, substrates, test capacity, and yield learning curves.
High-speed networking capacity across Ethernet/InfiniBand switches, NICs, DSPs, optical transceivers, lasers, and silicon photonics.
Data-center electrical infrastructure including transformers, switchgear, UPS systems, power management, generators, and liquid cooling.
Grid interconnection queues, available baseload or firm power, nuclear/gas/renewable project timelines, and local permitting.
Enterprise AI deployment friction: data quality, data governance, security, integration with legacy workflows, ROI measurement, and model reliability.
